pages.task: On log-log axes, what does the power law y = 3 × x^0.5 look like?
pages.why: Take logs of both sides. That gives log y = log 3 + 0.5 log x. On log-log axes that is a straight line. Its gradient is the power, 0.5. The 3 only sets where the line sits. So any power law draws a straight line on log-log axes.

pages.name: Lost volts
pages.text: This 12 V battery is drawn as two parts in one case. The [[emf]], E, is a fixed push of 12.60 V from the plates and acid. In series sits a small [[internal resistance]], r, of 7 mΩ. Current through r drops volts there, I × r. The line above r steps down by that much. So the terminals read E − Ir. At 50 A the lost volts are 0.35 V, and the voltmeter reads 12.25 V.

pages.name: At 100 A
pages.task: The load now draws 100 A. What do the terminals read?
pages.why: The lost volts are I × r = 100 × 0.007 = 0.70 V. The terminals read what is left, 12.60 − 0.70 = 11.90 V. Reading the emf there would over-read by 0.70 V.

pages.name: The load sets it
pages.text: With nothing connected, no current flows. Nothing is lost across r, so the voltmeter reads the emf, 12.60 V. The battery does not set the current. The load does. Its label shows its resistance, R, the terminal voltage divided by the current. A 0.245 Ω load draws 50 A. Less resistance lets more current through. A 0.119 Ω load draws 100 A, and the terminals sag to 11.90 V.

pages.name: Halve the load
pages.task: The load draws 50 A. Its resistance is halved. What happens?
pages.answer: The current nearly doubles, and the terminal voltage dips a little
pages.why: The current is E ÷ (R + r). R falls from 0.245 Ω to 0.123 Ω, and r stays at 0.007 Ω. So the current rises from 50 A to 97 A. That is nearly double, not quite, because r stays in the sum. More current loses more volts, so the terminals dip to 11.92 V.

pages.name: Two ratings
pages.text: This battery is rated at a slow, 20-hour discharge. At 5 A it runs 20 hours and gives 100 Ah. The clock and counter run fast. The run stops when the terminals fall to the end voltage, 10.50 V. A dot drops at the ampere-hours delivered. At 28 A it lasts only 2 hours and gives just 56 Ah. Why fewer? More current loses more volts across r, I × r. So the terminals start lower and reach the end voltage sooner, with charge still in the plates.

pages.name: How long at 25 A
pages.task: This 100 Ah battery carries a 25 A load. How long does it last?
pages.why: Dividing 100 Ah by 25 A says 4 hours. That treats the battery as a fixed tank. But 25 A is five times the 20-hour current. A faster draw gives fewer ampere-hours, so it runs flat sooner. Here it lasts about 2.3 hours.

pages.name: Peukert's rule
pages.text: Peukert's rule fits a straight line through the two ratings. It says the current to a power n, times the run time, stays the same. So 5ⁿ × 20 = 28ⁿ × 2. Divide both sides by 5ⁿ × 2. That leaves 5.6ⁿ = 10, because 28 ÷ 5 = 5.6. Taking logs finds n.

pages.name: Find n
pages.why: Take logs of both sides. The power comes down as a multiplier: n × log 5.6 = log 10. Divide both sides by log 5.6. So n = log 10 ÷ log 5.6 = 1 ÷ 0.748 = 1.34.

pages.name: Peukert's line
pages.text: Capacity is current × time. The rule makes the time go as the current to the power −n. So capacity goes as the current to the power 1 − n. On log-log axes that is a straight line through both ratings. Its gradient is 1 − n, about −0.34. A perfect battery has n = 1.00, the flat dashed line. Past 28 A the line is untested, so that part is shaded. Far past it, a real battery gives even less than the line.

pages.name: Read the line
pages.task: The load draws 25 A. What does the line give?
pages.answer: About 58 Ah, lasting about 2 hours 20 minutes
pages.why: The rule gives the run time as 20 × (5 ÷ 25)^1.34 = 2.3 hours. That is about 2 hours 20 minutes. Current times time gives 25 × 2.3, about 58 Ah. A battery monitor's default n of 1.25 would say 67 Ah. So use the battery's own ratings where you have them.

options: About 58 Ah, lasting about 2 hours 20 minutes

pages.name: Cold
pages.text: Cold hurts twice. It raises the internal resistance, and it cuts the capacity. A battery giving 100 per cent at 27 °C gives only about 50 per cent at −18 °C. Here the load draws 20 A. Say r doubles in the cold, to 14 mΩ. The lost volts grow from 0.14 V to 0.28 V. The line and every dot drop to half. The 20 A dot drops from 63 Ah to 31 Ah.

pages.name: Past the ratings
pages.task: At 100 A the line gives 36 Ah, in the shaded part. What should you expect from a real battery?
pages.why: The line is only a fit through two ratings, at 5 A and 28 A. 100 A is far past the faster one. At very high currents a real battery gives even less than a fixed n predicts. So expect less than 36 Ah. Trust the fit only between the ratings.

pages.name: Which lasts longer
pages.why: At 5 A and 27 °C the battery runs 20 hours. Cold halves its ampere-hours, so at −18 °C the same 5 A runs about 10 hours. 28 A at 27 °C is the 2-hour rating, 56 Ah. So the slow, cold run still lasts five times as long.

pages.name: A ship's battery
pages.task: A ship's 24 V emergency battery must stay within 12 per cent of 24 V through its discharge. That sets a floor of 21.1 V. Under the emergency load, which voltage must stay above it?
pages.why: Twelve per cent of 24 V is 2.88 V. So the band runs from 21.1 V to 26.9 V. The load gets the terminal voltage, E − Ir. The emf alone leaves out the lost volts. They grow with the current and in the cold. So the terminals must hold above 21.1 V at the full emergency load, right to the end of the discharge.
